Light: Shadows and Reﬂ ections 11 In the Western Ghat region of Maharashtra, Keshav spends part of his summer vacation at his friend Jatin’s grandparents’ village. Having lived in a big city, he ﬁ nds the forests, fresh air, sounds of gushing streams, and chirping birds a novel experience. However, for Keshav, the most fascinating sight is the dance of hundreds of ﬁ reﬂ ies at night, ﬂ ashing their lights in a wonderful performance. Jatin’s grandparents explain that ﬁ reﬂ ies are seasonal insects and they use light to communicate. Unfortunately, Keshav also learns the number of ﬁ reﬂ ies is decreasing due to light pollution, reduced forest cover, and excessive tourism. At the end of their vacation, Keshav and Jatin board an evening bus back to their city. As the bus winds through the hilly roads, Keshav watches the moonlit landscape and the beams from the headlights of passing vehicles ﬂ ashing by. He is reminded of the many poems and songs about moonlight, and wonders — does the Moon actually produce its own light? Did we not learn in the chapter ‘Beyond Earth’ in the Grade 6 Science textbook Curiosity that all other objects in our solar system shine only by reﬂ ecting the light of the Sun? Is moonlight just reﬂ ected sunlight? Which objects give oﬀ their own light? While thinking, he notices something strange — light seems to move in a straight line!

Place the pen in front of the mirror as shown in
Fig. 11.10.

Sources of Light

The Sun emits its own light and is the main natural source of light on Earth. Stars, lightning, fire, and certain animals also emit their own light. Objects that emit their own light are called luminous objects (like the Sun), while objects that do not emit light but reflect it are non-luminous objects (like the Moon). The Moon reflects sunlight; therefore, moonlight is reflected sunlight.

Types of Light Sources

Natural sources include the Sun, stars, lightning, and animals. Artificial sources include fire (using fuels like oil or gas), electric lamps, and LED lamps. LEDs are preferred because they consume less power, last longer, and reduce electricity bills.

Light Travels in a Straight Line

Experiments using matchboxes, torches, and bent pipes demonstrate that light travels in straight lines. When an object blocks the path of light, it creates a shadow because light cannot bend around corners.

Light Through Materials

Materials can be classified as transparent (allowing light to pass fully), translucent (allowing partial light passage), or opaque (blocking all light). A laser beam follows a straight path through water but can bend around corners in complex environments.

Light: Shadows and Reﬂ ections 11 In the Western Ghat region of Maharashtra, Keshav spends part of his summer vacation at his friend Jatin’s grandparents’ village. Having lived in a big city, he ﬁ nds the forests, fresh air, sounds of gushing streams, and chirping birds a novel experience. However, for Keshav, the most fascinating sight is the dance of hundreds of ﬁ reﬂ ies at night, ﬂ ashing their lights in a wonderful performance. Jatin’s grandparents explain that ﬁ reﬂ ies are seasonal insects and they use light to communicate. Unfortunately, Keshav also learns the number of ﬁ reﬂ ies is decreasing due to light pollution, reduced forest cover, and excessive tourism. At the end of their vacation, Keshav and Jatin board an evening bus back to their city. As the bus winds through the hilly roads, Keshav watches the moonlit landscape and the beams from the headlights of passing vehicles ﬂ ashing by. He is reminded of the many poems and songs about moonlight, and wonders — does the Moon actually produce its own light? Did we not learn in the chapter ‘Beyond Earth’ in the Grade 6 Science textbook Curiosity that all other objects in our solar system shine only by reﬂ ecting the light of the Sun? Is moonlight just reﬂ ected sunlight? Which objects give oﬀ their own light? While thinking, he notices something strange — light seems to move in a straight line!

FASCINATING FACTS

Sources of Light

The Sun emits its own light and is the main natural source of light on Earth. Stars, lightning, fire, and certain animals also emit their own light. Objects that emit their own light are called luminous objects (like the Sun), while objects that do not emit light but reflect it are non-luminous objects (like the Moon). The Moon reflects sunlight; therefore, moonlight is reflected sunlight.

Types of Light Sources

Natural sources include the Sun, stars, lightning, and animals. Artificial sources include fire (using fuels like oil or gas), electric lamps, and LED lamps. LEDs are preferred because they consume less power, last longer, and reduce electricity bills.

Light Travels in a Straight Line

Experiments using matchboxes, torches, and bent pipes demonstrate that light travels in straight lines. When an object blocks the path of light, it creates a shadow because light cannot bend around corners.

Light Through Materials

Materials can be classified as transparent (allowing light to pass fully), translucent (allowing partial light passage), or opaque (blocking all light). A laser beam follows a straight path through water but can bend around corners in complex environments.
